story: The red sandstone of the Constance Range and the eastern gorge was laid down as sand in a shallow sea about 1,560 million years ago, when life was little more than bacteria and stromatolites; ripple marks from that seabed still show in places. Around 530 million years ago another sea left grey limestone with sponges and trilobites. Lawn Hill Creek, fed by springs from the limestone plateau to the west, has cut down along fractures to make the gorge, and where its lime-rich water spills over obstacles it builds fragile tufa, as at Indarri Falls and the Cascades.

At Riversleigh, younger limestones laid down between 25 and 15 million years ago in small rainforest lakes hold innumerable fossils of the ancestors of Australia's animals, washed or fallen into those lakes. QPWS counts Riversleigh among the most significant fossil deposits in the world. The gorge itself is a corridor for wildlife and the eastern limit for the rock ringtail possum and the purple-crowned fairy-wren. The gulf snapping turtle was described from a Riversleigh fossil in 1994 and thought extinct, until a living one was caught in Lawn Hill Creek.

The Waanyi people are the Traditional Owners, and occupation at Lawn Hill goes back at least 17,000 years and perhaps beyond 30,000. They know this as Boodjamulla, Rainbow Serpent country: the serpent formed the gorge and made its permanent springs, and will leave and take the water if it is polluted or taken for granted. To the Waanyi the gorge is a sacred place for ceremony. Mussel middens, grindstones and rock art remain, and Waanyi Elders have interpreted some of these sites for visitors.

Cattle came to Lawn Hill Creek in the 1860s, and from the mid-1870s Frank Hann gathered up leases; by 1976, when the Brazilian cattleman Sebastiao Maia took it over, Lawn Hill Station covered 11,000 square kilometres, one of the largest cattle stations in Queensland. In 1984 Maia surrendered 12,200 hectares of Lawn Hill Station to the Queensland Government, and Lawn Hill Gorge was gazetted as a national park that December. Riversleigh was added in 1992 and inscribed on the World Heritage List in 1994. In 2023 the Queensland Government began returning the park to the Waanyi people.
howItWorks: Boodjamulla is Aboriginal land owned by the Waanyi people. At a ceremony on 23 June 2023 the first 79,000 hectares — including Lawn Hill Gorge and Riversleigh — were handed to the Waanyi Native Title Aboriginal Corporation, which leases the land back to the State in perpetuity to be managed as a national park. It was the first national park of its kind in Queensland, and it is managed jointly by the Waanyi people and the Queensland Parks and Wildlife Service through the Boodjamulla Cooperative Management Council. A further 167,400 hectares were handed back at a ceremony in Cairns in November 2025.

There is no entry fee, but every camp site must normally be booked before you arrive, and well ahead for Queensland school holidays and the April-to-October peak season. In November 2026 the Queensland booking system was switched off after a data breach at the provider Bookeasy; while the temporary arrangements last, QPWS says you may camp in open parks without a permit, although its Boodjamulla alert still calls bookings essential. Check the QPWS website and park alerts before you go.

Lawn Hill Gorge is still reopening in stages after major flooding. In November 2026 the Constance Range track, the Duwadarri lookout track (by a temporary link), the paddle to Indarri Falls and the Lawn Hill Gorge camping area were open; all other gorge tracks were closed for repairs, and on the creek you must leave the water where you entered. Riversleigh's D Site fossil trail and Miyumba camping area were open. Rangers may not be on site: you must be self-sufficient, and a satellite phone or personal locator beacon is recommended.

sightNotes.poi-au-boodjamulla-lawn-hill-gorge-canoe: Paddle the emerald water of Lawn Hill Creek between orange sandstone cliffs in the Middle Gorge, about 3 kilometres return to Indarri Falls, roughly an hour's paddling.
sightNotes.poi-au-boodjamulla-indarri-falls: A tufa waterfall across Lawn Hill Creek, built by lime-rich spring water. There is no landing at the falls; paddle back to the launch point.
sightNotes.poi-au-boodjamulla-constance-range-track: A grade 5 walk, 3.6 kilometres return and about three hours, beside the Lower Gorge and up onto the range's ridge tops for panoramic views. Start early to avoid the heat.
sightNotes.poi-au-boodjamulla-the-cascades: Tufa terraces on Lawn Hill Creek. Canoeing is not permitted here, to protect the formations; check park alerts for track access.
sightNotes.poi-au-boodjamulla-gregory-river-at-miyu: The year-round Gregory River beside Miyumba camping area, in the Riversleigh section, about 4 kilometres from the D Site fossil trail.

chronology.text: Aboriginal occupation at Lawn Hill is under way; it may reach back beyond 30,000 years.
Pastoralists bring the first cattle to the Lawn Hill Creek area.
Frank Hann buys up leases that grow into the Lawn Hill Riversleigh pastoral holding.
Sebastiao Maia takes over the lease of Lawn Hill Station, then about 11,000 square kilometres.
Maia surrenders 12,200 hectares to the Queensland Government, and Lawn Hill Gorge is gazetted as a national park in December.
The park is extended in March to take in Riversleigh.
Riversleigh and Naracoorte are inscribed together on the World Heritage List as the Australian Fossil Mammal Sites.
On 23 June more than 79,000 hectares are handed back to the Waanyi people and dedicated as Boodjamulla National Park (Aboriginal land).
A further 167,400 hectares are handed back at a ceremony in Cairns in November.

safety: The park is remote and rangers may not be on site. Be self-sufficient, carry a satellite phone or personal locator beacon, and know that mobile coverage is limited to patches of Telstra 4G.
Carry and drink at least 2 litres of water per person per day; Lawn Hill Creek water, high in calcium carbonate, makes you thirstier.
Freshwater crocodiles live in Lawn Hill Creek. They are timid but may bite if disturbed; do not approach them and take care if swimming.
Walk in the cool of the day, stay clear of cliff edges, and carry a torch at night, when snakes are active.
regulations: No fires; use a fuel or gas stove. Generators are not permitted.
Fishing is prohibited in Lawn Hill Creek, and motorised boats are banned. Canoeing is not permitted in the Cascades or the Lower Gorge.
Fossicking or interfering with fossils and rocks is illegal at Riversleigh; stay on the marked track. Respect Waanyi sacred places and do not enter them.
Drones are prohibited in camping areas and strongly discouraged elsewhere in the park. Domestic animals are prohibited.
There are no rubbish bins; take your rubbish with you. Do not empty chemical toilets into the composting toilets.

weather: North-west Queensland has two seasons. The dry, from May to September, brings clear skies and low humidity; in July days average about 28°C and nights 12°C, sometimes dropping to single figures. The wet, from October to April, brings heavy rain, high humidity and temperatures from 25 to 45°C, and January is the wettest month, averaging 147 millimetres. Heat radiating off the sandstone makes days hotter than the forecast suggests, so walk early and carry plenty of water.
directions: The park is on the Northern Territory border, far from any city. The only route suitable for conventional vehicles and off-road caravans runs 100 unsealed kilometres from Gregory Downs, 72 kilometres west along the Wills Developmental Road and 21 kilometres south on Riversleigh Road; a four-wheel drive is still recommended. From Mount Isa or Camooweal, drive the Barkly Highway to the Gregory–Burketown turn-off and continue on unsealed roads via Riversleigh — unsuitable for conventional vehicles and caravans. Rough four-wheel-drive routes also come in from the north via Hell's Gate or Doomadgee. Expect bulldust and corrugations, and check road conditions with the Department of Transport and Main Roads.
